claims.claim: Lagus finds Ship of Magic's internal focalization immersive and often pronounced.
claims.source: Timo Lagus, MA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2006
claims.quote: Its internal focalization is immersive and often pronounced

claims.claim: To exemplify Hobb's figural perspectivism Lagus reprints a domestic bedside passage in which the trader matriarch Ronica Vestrit, nursing her dying husband, weighs what to do about an indentured servant.
claims.source: Timo Lagus, MA thesis, University of Helsinki, 2006
claims.quote: Sitting by her dying husband's bedside, Ronica Vestrit, the matriarch
claims.page: ch. 5, pp. 126-127 (block quotation from Ship of Magic)

claims.claim: Moon describes the older narrating Fitz as a historian who keeps getting distracted by his own role in the history.
claims.source: Emily Moon, "'I set no limits on my love': Magic, Queerness and the Disruption of Binaries in Robin Hobb's Realm of the Elderlings", MA by Research, University of Kent, 2024
claims.quote: that of a historian getting distracted by their own role

claims.claim: Moon reads the sudden appearance and disappearance of quotation marks around a pronoun as the seam between the child Fitz's usage and the older narrator's.
claims.source: Emily Moon, MA by Research, University of Kent, 2024
claims.quote: the abrupt addition and disappearance of quotation marks

claims.claim: Susan Mandala, as relayed by Wikipedia, holds that Hobb writes the fantastic as an unquestioned, familiar part of the setting, producing an illusion of familiarity for the reader.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Farseer trilogy', Style section, relaying Susan Mandala, Language in Science Fiction and Fantasy: The Question of Style (Continuum, 2010) 100-102
claims.quote: casts the fantastic as an unquestioned, familiar aspect of the setting

claims.claim: Mandala, relayed by Wikipedia, observes that Hobb's narration of Fitz's first shared dream with a dog stays lexically coherent across the human and the animal parts.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Farseer trilogy', Style section, relaying Susan Mandala, Language in Science Fiction and Fantasy (2010) 101-102
claims.quote: the narration matches how he experiences the dream

claims.claim: When the Skill is first named, the narrative does not explain the term, treating its meaning as known inside the world.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Farseer trilogy', Style section, relaying Susan Mandala, Language in Science Fiction and Fantasy (2010) 102
claims.quote: the narrative does not address the term directly

claims.claim: Mandala, relayed by Wikipedia, notes that Fitz describes his own family in the same terms he uses for strangers, his grandfather becoming 'the tall man' and his mother 'a voice'.
claims.source: Wikipedia, 'Farseer trilogy', Style section, relaying Susan Mandala, Language in Science Fiction and Fantasy (2010) 128-130
claims.quote: Fitz describes his immediate family in the same terms as the

claims.claim: Wikipedia's Farseer article describes the chapter-prefacing excerpts as short memoirs narrating a fictional history of the setting, and calls them unreliable narratives.
claims.quote: short memoirs prefacing each chapter that narrate a fictional history

claims.claim: Elliott calls attention to the all-too-human factors of avarice and pettiness a hallmark of Hobb's writing, citing the looting of her memorial city by merchants.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'Sites of Memory in Robin Hobb's Realm of the Elderlings', paper given at the 2021 International Congress on Medieval Studies (Tales after Tolkien Society session), self-published 19 May 2021
claims.quote: the all-too-human factors of avarice and pettiness

claims.claim: Elliott reports that in Hobb's Bingtown a family buying a liveship commonly takes a multi-generational loan secured by potential marriages.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'Sites of Memory in Robin Hobb's Realm of the Elderlings' (ICMS 2021)
claims.quote: a multi-generational loan, secured by potential marriages, to purchase one
claims.page: section 'The Strange Sites of Memory: The Liveships'

claims.claim: Elliott notes that Hobb introduces the ruined city Kelsingra through what Fitz fails to perceive there.
claims.source: Geoffrey B. Elliott, 'Sites of Memory in Robin Hobb's Realm of the Elderlings' (ICMS 2021)
claims.quote: he finds it empty, perceiving no signs of life around him

claims.claim: Waumans, Nicodeme and Bersini's corpus of forty-seven best-selling novels includes seven of Hobb's - the three Liveship Traders and four Rain Wild Chronicles books.
claims.source: Michael C. Waumans, Thibaut Nicodeme and Hugues Bersini, 'Topology Analysis of Social Networks Extracted from Literature', PLoS ONE 10.6 (3 June 2015)

claims.claim: The study proposes dialogue spacing and alias-network topology as features that may identify an author's style.
claims.source: Waumans, Nicodeme and Bersini, PLoS ONE 10.6 (2015)
claims.quote: relevant in the identification of the author's style like the dialog

claims.claim: In the study's hierarchical clustering the Rain Wild Chronicles books cluster together, which the authors treat as an absence of the style fluctuation they see in a scattered series.
claims.source: Waumans, Nicodeme and Bersini, PLoS ONE 10.6 (2015)
claims.quote: The dendrogram shows a good clustering of certain series
